1:
Job opens his reply by insisting that the wisdom his friends have paraded is no news to him, for his own eye had "seen all this" and his ear had heard and understood it; and the witnesses read the boast as the ground of everything that follows. The reformed John Gill weighs the reach of the claim: Job's eye had seen the instances of God's power and wisdom he had been discoursing of, being an eyewitness to some and discerning others with the enlightened eyes of his understanding, so that he knew as much of these divine things as his friends did. Yet Gill will not press the words to the breaking-point; though they run absolutely, "my eye hath seen all things," they must not be taken in the largest sense of all that can be seen and known, for Job's knowledge, great as it was, did not compass everything, and many things in nature his eye had never seen. The claim is to a full share in the matter under debate, not to omniscience.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in it a man forced, as Paul was by the Corinthians, to commend his own knowledge, not in self-applause but in self-justification. All Job had said, his eye had seen confirmed by many instances and his ear had heard seconded by many authorities, and he well understood it and what use to make of it; happy, Henry adds, are those who not only see and hear but understand the greatness, glory, and sovereignty of God. And he draws the caution that hangs over the whole speech: those who enter into disputation enter into temptation to magnify themselves and vilify their brethren more than is fit, and ought to watch and pray against the workings of pride.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the sense plain. Adam Clarke puts the retort in a sentence, "Ye have brought nothing new to me; I know those maxims as well as you, nor have you any knowledge of which I am not possessed." John Wesley refers the "all this" to all that either Job or his friends had discoursed concerning the infinite power and wisdom of God, and marks the double source of Job's knowledge named in the verse itself: he knew it both by seeing it, by his own observation and experience, and by hearing it from his ancestors. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job here levels the ground of the argument, standing on no lower footing of knowledge than the men who have come to instruct him, and that this equal standing is precisely what entitles him, in the next breath, to turn from his friends to God.
2:
Having claimed to have seen and heard all his friends allege, Job presses the equality home, "what ye know, the same do I know also," and the witnesses gather around a boast that is really a plea. The reformed John Gill keeps it concrete: what Job knew was the same his friends knew concerning God and his perfections, his sovereignty, holiness, justice, wisdom, power, and goodness, and concerning his providences and dealings with men, whether in an ordinary or an extraordinary way. There is nothing in their store of divinity, Gill implies, that is not already in his.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology and the force. The first line, "mine ear hath heard and marked it," they read with the dative not as the Aramaic accusative of the object but as a dative of advantage, or even an ethical dative, the ear having made the matter intelligible to itself, the verb marking the apprehension that accompanies perception. The plain "all" they take here in the definite sense of "all this," the whole exalted majesty of God, of which Job has a knowledge acquired partly by his own observation and partly from the teaching of others; and "I am not inferior unto you" they render, he does not stand back behind them, having a knowledge equal to theirs. Job has, they note, already argued this at the head of the speech in ch. 12:3, and now repeats as proved what he there maintained.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, translates the clause "I fall not short of you," and then lifts the verse toward the whole drift of the book. It is this very sense of the inscrutableness of God's dealings, he says, that makes Job long to come face to face with God and to reason with Him on the first principles of His action. And Ellicott draws a striking lesson from the contest: since it is the traditionally orthodox position that the friends assume, it is refreshing to find that some truth may be spoken for God by what is not so reckoned, and that more ultimate truth may exist in honest doubt than is sometimes found in the profession of a loosely-held creed, quoting the Laureate, "There lives more truth in honest doubt, believe me, than in half the creeds." The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's parity of knowledge is not vanity but the warrant for his appeal, the ground on which a man who knows God as well as his accusers do may carry his cause past them to God himself.
3:
From the equal footing just claimed Job turns his back on his friends and sets his face toward heaven, his desire, as the verse has it, "to reason with God." The reformed John Gill reads the "surely" as a "therefore": since Job knew as much as his friends, and they no more than he, he would have no more to do with them as judges, but appeal to God and plead his own cause before him, not doubting a candid hearing. For Gill is careful that this is no mere language of prayer, though prayer too is a speaking to God in which he delights; it is the language of a man who knows that the Judge of all the earth will do right, will judge him according to his righteousness and integrity, and will in the end give the cause for him against his friends, as indeed he afterwards did.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the Hebrew particle as a wish, "O that," and hears the whole verse spoken with reference to a court of justice: "I wish I could speak to the Almighty; I desire to reason with God." The edge of it falls on the friends: "Ye pretend to be advocates for God, but ye are forgers of lies; O that God himself would appear! Before him I could soon prove my innocence of the evils with which ye charge me." John Wesley reads the same preference plainly, "I had rather debate the matter with God than with you," and grounds Job's boldness in his conscience: "I am not afraid of presenting my person and cause before him, who is a witness of my integrity."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers over the paradox that a man should sooner trust the Judge than the witnesses. Job could promise himself no satisfaction in talking to his friends, and longed rather for liberty to reason with God, who would not be so hard upon him as they were; the prince himself, Henry observes, will often give a poor petitioner a milder and more patient hearing than his servants will. And he draws out what such a longing reveals: what confidence those have toward God whose hearts do not condemn them of reigning hypocrisy, that they can with humble boldness appear before him and appeal to him; and what comfort those have in God whose neighbours unjustly condemn them, that though they may not be fairly heard by men, they may still speak to the Almighty, who gives them easy access and will accept them. The witnesses converge: Job's flight from his friends to God is not despair but the boldness of a clear conscience.
4:
"But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value" — the retort is the harshest word Job has yet flung, and the witnesses handle both its heat and its two images. The reformed John Gill owns the harshness: Job was in a passion, provoked by his friends, and retorts upon them the charge they had laid on him; so, he notes, in controversies between good men undue heats arise and unbecoming words drop out. To tell lies is bad, but to forge them, a studied, premeditated, contrived lie, is far worse. Yet Gill softens the accusation by a distinction: Job may not mean lies in the strict sense but falsehoods and untruths, for a man may deliver an untruth not knowing it to be such; or he may mean doctrinal lies, like the false prophets' untempered mortar, whereby they made sad the hearts of the righteous.

On the second image the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is fullest. "Physicians of no value" means feeble reasoners and inefficient healers: they can neither heal the wound of his mind nor the disease of his body. In ancient times every wise man professed skill in the healing art, and Job's friends had perhaps tried their skill on his body as well as his mind, so that his retort carries a double edge, forgers of lies in divinity, good-for-nothing physicians in physic. Clarke presses the first word too, deriving "forgers" from a root meaning to fasten or sew together, so that the imagery is surgical, and the friends are as much "chirurgeons of falsity" as worthless physicians; the Chaldee's "ye are idle physicians" keeps the same sense.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the terms as a measured payment in kind: Job retorts in language not more deferential than his friends' own, calling them patchers-up and botchers-together of falsehood, and physicians powerless to heal or even to understand the case, for he feels that they have failed, miserably and utterly, to understand him. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, set the line at the head of the strophe that runs to v.11, and name the fault beneath it: the friends have set themselves up as God's advocates and at the same time accept his person, an injustice to Job and an evil service rendered to God that will not escape his undisguised punishment. The witnesses do not divide over the sting; they only weigh, with Gill, whether "lies" be reckoned in the strict sense or softened to the untruths of men honestly mistaken.
5:
His accusers silenced would, Job says, be his accusers at their wisest, for holding their peace "should be your wisdom." The reformed John Gill reads the wish as regret that they had ever spoken: since what they said of him was neither true nor to the purpose, nor tended to the comfort of his afflicted soul but the reverse, he could wish they had never broken the silence they kept the first seven days; and now that they have spoken and done only harm, he desires that for the future they say no more.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears behind the line the proverb of Prov. 17:28, "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise; and he that shutteth his lips, a man of understanding," and takes the occasion for one of his standing opinions: there is no need to suppose Solomon borrowed from Job, for the saying is a general apophthegm found among the wise of all nations, and in Clarke's judgment the high antiquity commonly claimed for the book of Job is unfounded, Solomon being the likelier author, or at least the book not written till his day. A silent man, he adds, is not likely to be a fool, for a fool is always prating and a fool's bolt is soon shot; the Latins say the same, "a wise man speaks little."

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, agrees that the sentiment is "singularly like" the same proverb, and turns it neatly against the friends: their wisdom will consist not in displaying their own folly but in listening to Job's wisdom. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same thought and adds his own weight. It would be a credit to them, he says, to say no more, having said too much already: "Hold your peace, and it shall be your wisdom, for thereby you will conceal your ignorance and ill-nature." They had pleaded that they could not forbear speaking, but they would have consulted their own reputation better had they enjoined themselves silence; better say nothing than say what tends to the dishonour of God and the grief of a brother. And, Henry notes, silence is not only an evidence of wisdom but a means of it, for it gives a man time to think and to hear. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Job's grieved wish that his comforters, having lost the credit of good counsel, might at least keep the credit of holding their peace.
6:
If they will not be silent for their own sake, Job pleads, let them at least be silent enough to hear him: "hear now my reasoning, and hearken to the pleadings of my lips." The reformed John Gill marks the reversal Job asks, that his friends would be no longer speakers but hearers, vouchsafing to sit still and attend to what he had to say. Afflicted as he was, Job had not lost his reason; his wisdom was not driven out of him, but remained with him to be used, even before God, and he desires that they attend to his self-defence on his own behalf, with the same patience they had claimed for their own long speeches. He pleads not in the wildness of despair but in the order of reason, and asks that his reasoning be given a fair and deliberate ear; and though his cause seemed desperate in his friends' eyes, he was willing to have it weighed by the strictest measure, if only they would lay aside their prejudice and attend to what he said.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the setting that governs the whole chapter's vocabulary: the speeches here are conceived as delivered in a court of justice, with counsellors pleading against one another, so that most of the terms — "reasoning," "pleadings," "ordered my cause," "plead with me" — are forensic. Job is not merely venting grief; he is opening a case, and asks the court's ear for it, as a man confident that his brief will bear examination. The request is of a piece with all that follows, in which Job will conduct himself less as a sufferer bewailing his lot than as a defendant laying out his defence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the request as a claim of simple justice. Perhaps, though they did not interrupt his discourse, the friends seemed careless and did not much heed what he said; he therefore begs that they would not only hear but hearken. And Henry draws the general rule from it: we should be very willing and glad to hear what those have to say for themselves whom, upon any account, we are tempted to think hard thoughts of, for many a man, could he but be fairly heard, would be fairly acquitted even in the consciences of those that run him down. It is no small part of charity, Henry implies, to let an accused man speak, and no small part of wisdom to weigh what he says before condemning him. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job, having denied his friends the character of wise physicians, does not therefore refuse the forms of fair debate, but submits his cause to a hearing, asking of them the very patience they had denied him, and asking it in the confidence of a man who believes his reasoning will bear the light.
7:
Job now turns the tables on the friends' pretended zeal, asking whether men may lie for the God of truth: "will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?" The reformed John Gill unfolds the double fault. They spoke for God, pleading the honour of his justice by maintaining that he does not afflict good men; but in the same breath they spoke wickedly of Job, that being afflicted of God he must be a bad man and a hypocrite. This was to vindicate God's justice at the expense of his servant's character, and needlessly, Gill insists, for they might have upheld the honour of that justice and yet allowed both that God does afflict good men and that Job was such a one.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as an exposure of their method: to support their own cause, and in contradiction to the evidence of Job's whole upright life, they keep asserting that God could not thus afflict him unless flagrant iniquity were found in his ways; and so, in Clarke's stinging phrase, "ye tell lies for God's sake, and thus ye wickedly contend for your Maker."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears Job rise here to a sublime truth that shows how far he had climbed toward the true conception of God: that He who is no respecter of persons desires no favour to be shown to Himself, so that in seeking to flatter God the friends will only damage their own cause; for He is a God of truth, by whom words as well as actions are weighed, and nothing that is not true can stand any man in stead with Him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a maxim against pious fraud. God and his cause did not need such advocates, weak and passionate as they were; he is a God and can plead for himself, and were they for ever silent the heavens would declare his righteousness. Under pretence of justifying God they had condemned an innocent man, and that is speaking wickedly and talking deceitfully, for a good intention will neither justify nor sanctify a bad word: "God's truth needs not our lie, nor God's cause either our sinful policies or our sinful passions." Pious frauds, Henry concludes, are impious cheats, and devout persecutions horrid profanations of the name of God. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that partiality toward God is itself an offence against the God of truth.
8:
"Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God?" — and the witnesses fasten on the strange charge that a man might be guilty of partiality toward the Almighty himself. The reformed John Gill draws the courtroom sense: to accept persons is what earthly judges must never do, giving a cause to one through favour or affection to his person, because he is rich or a friend, and against another. Something like this, Job intimates, the friends had done, considering only what God was, holy, just, wise, and good, and so far right, yet attending to that alone and wholly neglecting the cause of Job itself, giving it against him because he was poor, abject, and miserable; and this looked like a respecting of persons.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in its strophe and name the offence: the friends set themselves up as God's advocates and at the same time "accept his person," as one accepts a gratifying gift, a partiality that God, who searches, will not leave unpunished. The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen it. Adam Clarke asks whether they think to act by God as by a mortal, and "by telling lies in his favour, attempt to conciliate his esteem"; John Wesley glosses "accept his person" as judging not according to the right of the cause but according to the quality or the person.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the irony that God's professed champions do his cause the most harm. They valued themselves on being of counsel for the sovereign, and expected the last word and judgment on their side; but God's cause is so just that it needs no such methods for its support. "Will you contend for God," Henry has Job ask, "as if his justice were clouded and wanted clearing up, or as if he were at a loss and wanted you to speak for him?" Good work ought not to be put into bad hands; he is a God and can plead for himself (Judg. 6:31), and if they were for ever silent the heavens would declare his righteousness. To condemn a man their own consciences might acquit, under colour of magnifying God, is to make his cause suffer by their management. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that to flatter the Judge is to insult him, and that the friends' advocacy, however well meant, is an affront to the very justice it pretends to serve.
9:
Job would have his friends turn their inquisition upon themselves and ask how they would fare under God's: "is it good that he should search you out?" The reformed John Gill takes the searching in a judicial sense, ascribed to God after the manner of men, though he needs no such diligence to find anything out; it is done not for his own sake but to lay men open. He borrows the proverb that "he that is first in his own cause seemeth just, but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Prov. 18:17): the friends, making the best of their own case and the worst of Job's, seemed right in their own eyes, but God, the searcher of hearts, would traverse their arguments and show the fallacy of them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the question straight upon their conscience: would it be to their credit if God should try their hearts and uncover the motives of their conduct? Were they tried as Job was, how would they appear? And the second clause he reads as a warning against thinking God as easily imposed on as a man: "Do ye think that you can deceive him, and by flattering speeches bring him to your terms, as you would bring an undiscerning, empty mortal like yourselves?" The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses the mockery with precision, "as one man, with mingled flattery and deception, seeks to impose upon another," so that the sin is the attempt to cajole omniscience.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both halves as a summons to self-examination. It concerns us all, he says, seriously to consider whether it will be to our advantage or no that God searches the heart. To an upright man who means honestly it is good that God should search him, and therefore he prays for it, "Search me, O God, and know my heart," for God's omniscience is then a witness of his sincerity; but it is bad for the man who looks one way and rows another to be searched out and laid open to his confusion. And to think to mock God, Henry adds, is to be deceived, for those who imagine they can put a cheat upon him will find they have only cheated themselves; God is not mocked. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the friends, so ready to search Job, had never turned the candle of the Lord upon their own breasts, where its light would have discomposed them.
10:
The bare possibility of partiality becomes, in this verse, a certainty of rebuke: "he will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons." The reformed John Gill dwells on the doubled Hebrew, "in reproving he will reprove you": it may be depended on and expected, for God never suffers sin to go unreproved or uncorrected, and will do it to the purpose, with the sharpness the crime requires. Gill runs through the instruments of that reproof, by his Spirit, convincing of sin, righteousness, and judgment; by his word, written for reproof and correction; by his ministers, whose work it is to rebuke, sometimes with a needful sharpness; and by his providences, the afflictive dispensations with which he rebukes, whether in love, as he chastens his own children, or in wrath and hot displeasure, as here.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the warning short and heavy: they may expect from God not only his disapprobation but his hot displeasure. The stress in both readings falls on that word "secretly": it is the hidden partiality, the accepting of persons in the heart and not merely in the open verdict, that God will drag into the light and reprove. Gill presses the point that the reproof here designed is not the gentle chastening of love but the sharper rebuke of displeasure, such as the nature of the crime deserves; for a man may impose on his fellows and never be found out, but with God the concealment is itself part of the offence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the verse its edge of terror and its severity. If the friends do accept persons, though but secretly and in heart, God will be so far from being pleased with their censures of Job, even under colour of vindicating himself, that he will resent them as a great provocation, as any prince or great man would if a base action were done under the sanction of his name and under colour of advancing his interest. And Henry draws the sober rule that stands over the whole: what we do amiss we shall certainly be reproved for, one way or other, one time or other, though it be done ever so secretly. The very service the friends thought to render God, Henry adds, becomes, when it wrongs a brother, the ground of their own arraignment. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the God whom the friends thought to serve by their partiality is the very God who will call that partiality to a strict account, and that no plea of good intention will screen a secret respecting of persons from his rebuke.
11:
From the certainty of rebuke Job passes to the majesty that should have forestalled it: "shall not his excellency make you afraid, and his dread fall upon you?" The reformed John Gill unfolds the excellency into its several senses. There is an excellency in the very name of God, fearful and dreadful; in his nature and perfections, his power, justice, and holiness, in which he is glorious and tremendous, and which should deter men from sinning against him; and in his works of nature and providence, which show him near at hand and able in a moment to take vengeance. The word, Gill notes, may also be rendered "his height," his superiority to all beings, for he is the Most High, higher than the highest of men and above all that are called gods; or "his lifting up," as the Targum adds, upon a throne of judgment, whence he judges the whole earth in righteousness.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reduces the whole to a single dread stroke: the very apprehension of God's wrath is sufficient to crush them to nothing. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the verse spoken by a man who himself lived in the fear he presses on others. He would have the friends consider what a God he is into whose service they had thrust themselves, and if they would duly stand in awe of his terror they would not do the thing that made them obnoxious to his wrath. "You that have great knowledge of God, and profess religion and a fear of him, how dare you talk at this rate and give yourselves so great a liberty of speech? Ought you not to walk and talk in the fear of God?" (Neh. 5:9).

There is in God, Henry says, a dreadful excellency: he is the most excellent Being, and his excellencies are in themselves amiable and lovely, yet, considering man's distance from him by nature and his degeneracy by sin, his very power, holiness, justice, and goodness become dreadful, so that a holy awe of them should fall upon us and make us afraid to offend. And this, he adds, Job speaks as one who did himself know the terror of the Lord and lived in a holy fear of him, whatever his friends suggested to the contrary. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the men who set themselves up as God's counsel had forgotten the awe that His majesty demands of every creature presuming to speak in His name.
12:
Job caps his rebuke of the friends by weighing their vaunted wisdom and finding it dust: "your remembrances are like unto ashes, your bodies to bodies of clay." The reformed John Gill offers the range of what the "remembrances" may be: the mementos they had pressed upon him, the arguments and objections drawn out of their memories, their "memorable sentences," of no more moment than ashes and as easily blown away; or the memorials by which men hope to outlive themselves, houses and lands, wealth and honour, learning and knowledge, all of which fade and come to nothing. The memory of the just alone is blessed; all else that passes for a man's remembrance is but ashes, of little worth and soon trampled underfoot, and men should remember, as Aben Ezra says, that they are themselves but dust and ashes.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh both clauses. Adam Clarke renders the first, "your memorable sayings are proverbs of dust," aimed at the ancient wise saws they had heaped against Job; and the second he turns to their arguments, "your swelling heaps are swelling heaps of mire," their high-flown speeches dark, involved, and incoherent, all sound and no sense. John Wesley reads "remembrance" as that which is mouldering and coming to nothing, and takes the consideration of our mortality as the very point: it should make us afraid of offending God, their mementos being like ashes, contemptible and unprofitable.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse, "your memorable words are proverbs of dust, your strongholds are become strongholds of clay," calling the friends' warnings sayings to which attention and thought should be given. Charles Ellicott gives both possible parallelisms, "wise and memorable saws of garnered wisdom are proverbs of ashes, worthless as the dust, and fit for bodies of clay like your bodies," or else, taking the second line independently, "your high fabrics, or defences, are fabrics of clay." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in it a call to humility on both sides, for the consideration of our own meanness and mortality should make us afraid of offending God and keep us from despising and trampling on our brethren; and he records Bishop Patrick's turn of the verse, "your remonstrances on God's behalf are no better than dust, and the arguments you accumulate but so many heaps of dirt." The witnesses do not finally divide; whether the ashes be the friends' memorable sayings or their own frail bodies, all read the verse as Job's reminder that the men who spoke so grandly for God were themselves creatures of clay, whose wisdom would crumble with the frame that held it.
13:
Turning from rebuke to resolve, Job asks only for room to speak, come what may: "let me alone, that I may speak, and let come on me what will." The reformed John Gill catches the immediate occasion: Job could perceive by some motions of his friends that they were about to interrupt him, and so desires that they be silent and let him go on. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the opening, "be silent from me," that is, stand away and leave me in peace; then, and he alone, will he defend the cause his friends have so unkindly abandoned against their better knowledge, and let happen to him whatever may happen, "quidquid est," whatever it may be.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the close of the quarrel and the opening of the defence: "You have perverted righteousness and truth, and your pleadings are irrelevant; it is high time you should have done. I will now defend myself against you, and leave the cause to its issue." Charles Ellicott, another grammatical-historical voice, hears Job bracing himself for a declaration like the great one to come in chapter 19: he resolves, at all hazards, to face God in judgment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry opens here the long meditation that carries to the end of the speech, and reads the verse as Job taking fast hold of his integrity and refusing to let it go. He entreats his friends and all the company to let him alone and not interrupt what he is about to say, and to hearken diligently, for none but God and himself knew his heart, and he would have his own protestation be decisive. He resolves to speak in his own defence and let come on him what will, let his friends put what construction they please upon it and think the worse of him; he hopes God will not make his necessary defence to be his offence, as they do. And Henry draws the note that governs the whole: those who are upright, and have the assurance of their uprightness, may cheerfully welcome every event; come what will, with a heart well prepared they are ready for it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's demand for silence is not the petulance his friends took it for but the settled purpose of a man who, having committed his cause to God, is willing to abide any issue rather than betray his conscience by keeping still.
14:
The verse is a knot of proverb and grammar, and the witnesses pull at both: "wherefore do I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in mine hand?" The reformed John Gill reads the first clause as a figure for holding in his words, "or bite my lips, to keep in my words, and refrain from speaking? I will not do it." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat it as a proverbial phrase that occurs nowhere else, and render it of a man intent on the maintenance of his life as a wild beast is bent on preserving its prey, holding it fast between the teeth to carry it off; and they take the parallel clause, to put one's life in one's hand, in the sense it always bears elsewhere, to expose one's life to the greatest danger, as in the risks of Judg. 12:3 and 1 Sam. 19:5.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole as a settled proverb of daring: "I risk everything on the justice of my cause; I put my life in my hand; I run all hazards; I am fearless of the consequences," comparing the desperate courage of 1 Sam. 28:21. John Wesley gives it a more inward turn, making it the reason for Job's craving to speak: he could hold his tongue no longer, but must needs tear himself to pieces if he had no vent for his grief; and to have one's life in one's hand, he notes, denotes a condition extremely dangerous.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would settle the difficulty by refusing the question altogether: the verse, he argues, should not be read interrogatively but as a bold resolve, "at all risks, come what come may, I will take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in mine hand." So a genuine difference of reading runs beneath the line: whether Job asks, wonderingly, why he should thus imperil himself by speaking, as Gill and Keil and Delitzsch take it, or declares, defiantly, that he will do so and hang the danger, as Ellicott would have it. The witnesses do not divide over the sense of the images, self-endangerment for the sake of the truth he must utter, but only over the mood, whether the man marvels at his own daring or announces it. Either way the verse measures the cost Job knows he is running: that to plead his integrity before God may be to court the death he already half expects.
15:
"Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him" — the most famous line of the chapter, and the one over which the witnesses divide most sharply, for its first half turns on a single disputed Hebrew word. The reformed John Gill lays the textual fact bare. There is a double reading: the Keri, or marginal reading, is "in him," which the Authorized Version follows, "though he slay me, yet will I trust in him"; but the Ketib, or textual reading, is "not," which many follow, rendering the words, "lo, he will slay me, I shall not hope," or "I have no hope" of any other issue than to be slain. And this second sense, Gill allows, agrees with various expressions elsewhere in which Job professes he had no hope of a long life or of restoration to health.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm that the verse is one of a fixed list of eighteen passages in which the Ketib is the negative and the Keri the pronoun, Job 6:21 being another, so that the ambiguity is a recognized crux of the Masoretic text, their own rendering keeping the trust. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke weighs the manuscripts and comes down firmly for that traditional rendering. The common printed Hebrew has the negative, "I will not hope"; but the Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee all read the pronoun, "him," and with them agree twenty-nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts and the Complutensian and Antwerp Polyglots, so that "our translators have followed the best reading." Clarke paraphrases it as the very summit of trust: "I have no dependence but God; I trust in him alone. Should he even destroy my life by this affliction, yet will I hope that when he has tried me, I shall come forth as gold." He records too the older, gloomier turn of Coverdale, "Lo, there is nether comforte ner hope for me, yf he wil slaye me."

Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the case for the Ketib. The familiar rendering, he says, is "almost proverbial," but its accuracy is "very doubtful," for the better reading does not warrant it, but runs, "Behold, he will slay me; I have no hope; yet will I maintain my ways before him." We thus lose a very beautiful and familiar resolve, Ellicott grants, but the expression of living trust is not on that account less vivid: for though there is, and can be, no gleam of hope for victory in this unequal conflict, Job will still not forego his conviction of integrity, since the voice of conscience is the voice of God, and to renounce his innocence, knowing himself innocent, would be to belie and dishonour God as well as himself.

So the debate is genuine and unresolved: whether Job cries, in triumphant faith, "yet will I trust in him," or, in a darker and no less devout defiance, "I have no hope, yet will I maintain my ways." On the second clause all agree. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, keeping the received reading, calls the whole a high expression of faith that we should all labour to come up to, to trust God though he slay us, and to be well pleased with him as a friend even when he seems to come forth as an enemy. And Gill and Clarke join in reading the closing words as the settled resolve of a clear conscience: whatever the first half yields, Job will "maintain mine own ways before him," so conscious of his innocence that he does not fear to defend it in the very presence of his Maker.
16:
Job grounds his bold resolve in a deeper confidence, that the God he will face is also the God who saves him: "he also shall be my salvation: for an hypocrite shall not come before him." The reformed John Gill is careful to say what Job does and does not rest on. Though he asserts the integrity of his heart and life, he does not depend on his own ways and works for salvation, but on the Lord himself; and this is not the temporal deliverance of which Job had little hope, but a spiritual and eternal salvation, contrived by the Father and effected by the Son. Every soul sensible of its own insufficiency will resolve, as Job here, that God, and God only, shall be his Saviour; and Job knew him as his Saviour and living Redeemer, and would acknowledge no other, claiming his interest in him now and hereafter as his great support under all his troubles.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the second clause as the very proof of Job's sincerity: "He will save me, because I trust in him; a wicked man shall never be able to stand before him. I am conscious of this, and were I, as you suppose, a secret sinner, I should not dare to make this appeal." The confidence to come before God is itself the mark that he is no hypocrite. Keil and Delitzsch, another grammatical-historical voice, keep the forensic frame, taking Job's confession and declaration as the case he is eager to lay before God, the proof of an innocence he longs to have heard.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the verse the hinge of the whole book's portrait of Job. It is characteristic of him that, living as he probably did outside the pale of Israel, he nevertheless shared the faith and knowledge of God's chosen people; and this, Ellicott says, distinguishes Job most markedly from his friends: he can and does trust God unreservedly, in spite of all adverse circumstances, while they remain ignorant of the great central fact that God is himself the sinner's hope, and rest content on vague generalities. Because he has said, and can say, "He is and will be my salvation," he can also say, "I know that I shall be justified, because I trust in Him," the faith reckoned for righteousness in Genesis 15:6. We do not, Ellicott adds, import the Gospel into Job, but exhibit in Job what was already manifest in Abraham. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the man who dares to face God does so because he has already made God his refuge, and that his very willingness to appear is the evidence that he is no hypocrite.
17:
Job renews his plea for a hearing, as if he saw his listeners already turning away: "hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears." The reformed John Gill reads the doubled Hebrew, "in hearing hear," as a request not merely that they attend but that they continue to attend, and hear him out to the end. Upon his expressing so much faith and confidence in God, Gill suggests, the friends might well have risen from their seats, impatient that a man they took for a hypocrite should speak so boldly, or have broken in upon him mid-sentence; and so he presses them to be still, and to give diligent and patient ear to what he has yet to say, since the weightiest part of his cause is still to come. Job had told them their memorable sayings were but ashes; he does not therefore claim that his own words are idle, but stakes so much upon them that he begs they be weighed to the last syllable.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks the place of the verse in the structure of the speech: here Job "comes more closely to his business, the foregoing verses being mostly by way of preface." All that has gone before, the rebuke of the friends, the turning to God, the settling of terms, has been introduction; now the pleading itself begins, and Job asks for the concentrated attention the matter deserves, as a man who has cleared his throat of complaint and is ready to state his case.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the appeal, "hear, O hear my confession, and let my declaration echo in your ears," and give the two nouns their weight: the confession is the case Job will lay down, and the declaration the evidence he will bring in proof of his innocence, the latter a rare word found in the Hebrew of the Old Testament only in the book of Job. The very word for the confession, they observe, is one that in kindred usage comes to stand for religion itself, so solemn is the profession Job is about to make. The verse, on their reading, is not a mere call for silence but the formal opening of a defence, the moment at which the accused asks the court to mark every word. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, having cleared the ground and named his confidence, now stakes everything on being heard, and asks of his friends the one thing a man pleading for his life may fairly ask, that they listen, and keep listening, to the very end.
18:
Now the defence proper begins, and Job speaks like a man who has drawn up his brief: "behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified." The reformed John Gill unfolds the legal image: Job had looked over his cause afresh, reviewed the state of his case, considered it in every light, drawn a plan of it, and arranged his reasons and arguments in a regular form, so that he had them at hand and ready to produce, and upon the whole could draw this confident conclusion in the strongest terms. The word rendered "cause," Gill notes, is a word of judgment, and Job speaks as one who has ordered his brief and can rest the verdict on it. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the same courtroom note. Adam Clarke: "I am now ready to come into court, and care not how many I have to contend with, provided they speak truth." John Wesley: "I have seriously considered the state of my case, and am ready to plead my cause."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the pair, "I have arranged the cause; I know that I shall maintain the right," and carry the confidence forward into the challenge of the next verse, "who then can contend with me?" The ordering of the cause and the certainty of the verdict are, for them, one movement of a man sure of his ground.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry probes what such certainty rests on. Job knew he should be justified, Henry says, because he knew that his Redeemer lived (ch. 19:25); and those whose hearts are upright with God, walking not after the flesh but after the Spirit, may be sure that through Christ there shall be no condemnation to them, but that, whoever lays anything to their charge, they shall be justified, they may know that they shall. Yet Henry is careful to distinguish this from a claim of sinless perfection: Job does not say he can justify every word he has spoken, but that his cause, in the main, is good, and that a God who searches the heart will not find in him the reigning hypocrisy his friends allege. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's assurance is not presumption but the peace of a settled conscience, a man who has marshalled his case and can leave the issue to a righteous Judge, confident, as Henry puts it, that God will not make his necessary defence to be his offence.
19:
His brief in order, Job throws down a challenge and binds his very life to it: "who is he that will plead with me? for now, if I hold my tongue, I shall give up the ghost." The reformed John Gill hears in the challenge a man daring any comer to enter the lists and try the strength of his arguments; and he sets it, characteristically, in a wider frame, for the words fit the head of the church and the surety of his people, represented as speaking when he had made satisfaction and been justified as a public person, and fit too the believer in him who stands acquitted of every charge that men or devils, the law or his own unbelieving heart, can bring. Job, knowing the uprightness of his heart and the justness of his cause, boldly challenges his friends to come forth and try it, or rather, Gill thinks, is desirous that God himself would take the case in hand and plead with him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the summons of a defendant sure of acquittal: "Let my accuser, the plaintiff, come forward; I will defend my cause against him." And the second clause he takes of Job's utter absorption in the trial, "I shall cease to breathe; defending myself will be as respiration unto me," or else, while his adversary states the case, "I will be so silent as scarcely to appear to breathe."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds in the same clause a marvellous confession, and reads it as the very equation of Job's faith and his integrity: "if I hold my tongue, I shall give up the ghost" means, if I give up my faith in him who is my salvation, and the personal innocence that goes hand in hand with it, I shall perish; to give up my innocence is to give up him in whom I hold my innocence, and in whom I live. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it more simply as Job's resolve not to be silenced: if he holds his tongue and does not speak for himself, his silence now will for ever silence him, for he shall certainly give up the ghost; if he cannot be cleared, let him at least be eased by what he says. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job has staked his life on being heard, so that to keep still would not be patience but a kind of death, a surrender of the very conscience by which he lives.
20:
The challenge to his friends gives way, without a break, to a petition to God, on two plain conditions: "only do not two things unto me: then will I not hide myself from thee." The reformed John Gill notes the turn of address that the modesty of the verse half conceals: this is spoken not to Zophar in God's place but to God himself, for Job's whole desire had been to speak to the Almighty and have done with his friends; and before the pleadings begin on either side he is anxious to settle the terms and conditions of the dispute, requesting that two things be granted him, which the next verse will name. It is a delicate touch, Gill implies, that Job names God only indirectly, "do not two things unto me," rather than presume to arraign him openly; the very form of the petition owns whose hand it is that presses him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the two conditions and the reasons behind them. The first is, "withdraw thine hand far from me," remove the heavy affliction thy hand has inflicted; the second, "let not thy dread make me afraid," terrify me not with dreadful displays of thy majesty. And the reasons, Clarke says, are evident: how can a man plead for his life in a court of justice while under grievous bodily affliction? and how can he be recollected and self-possessed when overwhelmed by the awful appearance of the judge, the splendour of the court, and the ensigns of justice? The two requests, then, answer to the two things that would unfit any man for the trial — pain in the body and terror in the mind.

The grammatical-historical voices attend to the wording. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse with the two conditions Job had already named in ch. 9:34, that God grant him a respite from his troubles, and not overwhelm him with his majesty, the chastening hand that lies so heavily on him being the very thing that would prevent his pleading. Charles Ellicott glosses the closing clause with precision: "then will I not hide myself from thee" means "I shall not be hidden," a different word from the hiding of Adam in Genesis 3:10, though the comparison of the two places is not without interest. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job asks no favour in the verdict, only a fair field for the trial, that his body be eased of its torment and his mind of its terror, so that he may meet God not as a man crushed and cowering but as one able to state his cause and abide the answer.
21:
The two conditions are now spelled out, and the witnesses take them in turn: "withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid." The reformed John Gill reads the first as a plea against the pressure of pain: it is God's afflicting hand that presses Job, and unless it be removed he cannot command himself, make use of his reasoning faculties, recollect his arguments, or give them their due force; for afflictions of body affect the soul, the memory, the understanding, and the judgment, so that a man racked with pain can neither recollect his arguments nor urge them with their proper weight. This, Gill says, is the first of the things Job would have agreed before the dispute is entered on, the bare condition without which no reasoning is possible.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley joins the two petitions in one breath: "Suspend my torments during the time of my pleading with thee, that my mind may be at liberty; do not present thyself to me in terrible majesty, neither deal with me in rigorous justice." The first asks relief of pain, the second forbearance of terror, and both are asked only for the space of the trial; Job does not beg to escape the reckoning, but only that it be held on terms a mortal can bear.

The grammatical-historical voices sharpen the sense. Charles Ellicott paraphrases the whole, "cease to torture me bodily, and to terrify me mentally; let me at least have freedom from physical pain and the undue apprehension of thy terrors." Keil and Delitzsch note that the chastening hand of God is usually named by one word, and yet the term here, though it more often means the open palm, must be understood of that same heavy hand of God which lies upon Job, the painful pressure of which would otherwise prevent his answering when God should call. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's request is not for acquittal but for competence, for the bare conditions under which a suffering man may reason at all, and that he asks God, in effect, to lay aside for a moment both the rod and the terror, and meet him on ground where a mortal can stand and speak. It is the request of a man who does not fear the verdict but only his own inability, under torment, to make his case heard.
22:
With his two conditions asked, Job offers God the choice of roles in the coming trial: "then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me." The reformed John Gill sets out the alternatives as a courtroom would: either God may call Job by name in open court, or arraign him at the bar and exhibit his charges, and Job will answer them and clear himself; or else, if God will take the part of defendant, Job will be plaintiff, state his case, and receive God's reply. Either way he is ready, asking only that the pleadings be fairly ordered between them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse to the same effect, "call then, and I will answer, or I will speak, and answer thou me," and read it as the last of the terms Job lays down, following on the two petitions of the preceding verses: God is to grant him relief and forbearance, and then to open the cause, whether by questioning or by hearing. It is the language of a man confident that, given a fair field, he can meet whatever is brought against him.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley alone sounds a warning note over the boldness. This proposal, he says, "savoured of self-confidence, and of irreverence towards God," for which, and the like speeches, Job is afterwards reproved by God himself in ch. 38:2-3 and following. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both the boldness and its limits together: Job was well assured of the goodness of his cause and doubted not to have the comfort of it at last, and was ready either to hear God speak and return an answer, or to speak and expect an answer; yet Henry sees in the very request how hard a thing it is to have the great work of reasoning with God to do upon a bed of pain and under the terror of his majesty, and what a folly it is for any man to put off his repentance to a sick-bed and a death-bed. With such holy boldness, Henry says, may the upright come to the throne of grace, not doubting to find mercy there. The witnesses do not divide over Job's readiness; they differ only in tone, Wesley hearing an over-confidence that God will rebuke, Henry a boldness that, tempered by reverence, becomes the very access of an upright man to his God.
23:
"How many are mine iniquities and sins? make me to know my transgression and my sin" — with these words Job opens his direct pleading with God, and the witnesses hear in the heaped-up terms a demand at once humble and pointed. The reformed John Gill notes that by this heap of words, iniquities, sins, transgression, Job means all sorts of sins, of ignorance or presumption, of heart, lip, or life, and asks to know them both in quality and quantity, how great and how many they are; for his friends had made them, in effect, infinite. Yet Gill records Schultens's shrewd turn, that the interrogation carries the force of a diminution or even a negation, like the psalmist's "how many are the days of thy servant?" — that is, how few — so that Job may be representing his sins as few in comparison with the affliction laid on him.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read it as a demand for the bill of particulars. Adam Clarke: since it was a fact that Job was grievously afflicted, and his friends asserted this must be for grievous iniquity, he first desires to have the charges specified, "to say I must be a sinner to be thus afflicted is saying nothing; tell me what the sins are, and show me the proofs." John Wesley puts the confession and the challenge together: "That I am a sinner, I confess; but not that I am guilty of such crimes as my friends suppose; if it be so, do thou, O Lord, discover it."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is careful to hold the two sides of Job together: alongside his claim to be righteous there runs as deep a confession of personal sin, so that his declarations can only be understood in the light of that teaching which convicts of sin before it convinces of righteousness. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the request three ways, as a passionate complaint of hard usage, that he is punished for faults he is never told, or as a prudent appeal to God from the censures of his friends, whose judgment is not according to truth as God's is, or, best, as a pious request like that which Elihu would later urge (ch. 34:32), "that which I see not, teach thou me." A true penitent, Henry says, is willing to know the worst of himself, and we should all desire to know what our transgressions are, that we may be particular in confessing them and on our guard against them for the future. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job neither denies his sinfulness nor accepts his friends' indictment, but carries the question past them to the only Judge whose reckoning is according to truth.
24:
"Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy?" — the cry lifts Job's complaint from his body to his soul, and the witnesses feel the deeper wound in it. The reformed John Gill sets aside the lighter senses, that God hides his face from Job's cry, or from saving him, or from regarding his right ways, and takes it of God's withdrawing the manifestation of his face and favour: Job had formerly seen the face of God, enjoyed his presence, and walked in fellowship with him, but now God had hidden himself, and Job knew not where to find him. No greater blessing can be had than the gracious presence of God, Gill says, and nothing is more grievous to a good man than its being withheld; sin is often the cause, but not always, as here, where the Lord's end in all these afflictions, inward and outward, was to try Job's patience, integrity, and faithfulness.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear the perplexity of a conscience that cannot square the affliction with the justice of God. Job is conscious of having often prayed, "Remember not the sins of my youth" (Ps. 25:7); and yet he can only regard his suffering as the entailed inheritance of those early sins, since he knows of no sins of his riper years that should incur such wrath, and he cannot reconcile it with God's justice that He should again record against him what he had repented of. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the two clauses as two stabs of the same grief: "Why is it that I no longer enjoy thy approbation? Treatest me as if I were the vilest of sinners?"

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry insists that this is the sorest of Job's troubles, and something more than his outward losses. The loss of estate, children, and health might well consist with God's love, and when that was all, he had blessed the name of the Lord; but here his soul was sorely vexed, the favours of the Almighty suspended, God hiding his face as one displeased and strange to him, and the terrors of the Almighty inflicted, God holding him for an enemy and setting him as a mark for his arrows (ch. 6:4). The Holy Spirit, Henry observes, sometimes denies his favours and discovers his terrors to the best and dearest of his saints; a wounded spirit who can bear? And he reads Job's very sufferings as typical of the sufferings of Christ, from whom not only men hid their faces (Isa. 53:3) but God hid his, in the darkness of the cross and the cry, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the hiding of God's face, and not the boils or the losses, is the true depth of Job's misery, and that the man who can still call the God who wounds him his salvation is enduring the hardest of all trials, the felt withdrawal of the very presence he loves.
25:
Job pleads his own frailty as a reason for God to relent: "wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble?" The reformed John Gill draws out the image: a leaf fallen in autumn, withered, curled, and driven about by a wind it cannot resist, is what Job makes himself under the afflicting hand of God. He is careful that this is said not of Job's spiritual estate, for a good man is like a tree planted by rivers of water, whose leaf does not wither, unlike the carnal professor who in autumn casts his leaves and rotten fruit; it is of Job's outward frailty and feebleness that the figure is drawn, and especially of his weakness now under the afflicting hand of God. He recalls that even John the Baptist, as a frail mortal, was likened to a reed shaken with the wind. To break or pursue so weak a thing, Gill says, is but to add affliction to affliction, and could not well be borne.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the plea into a question of God's dignity: "Is it becoming thy dignity to concern thyself with a creature so contemptible?" — as if to say that so great a God gains no honour by crushing so slight a thing. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the very image a confession that borders on despair, noting that in comparing himself to a driven leaf and dry stubble Job approaches the language in which the psalmist describes the condition of the ungodly, blown away like chaff (Ps. 1:4).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as a humble pleading of Job's utter inability to stand before God. "Wilt thou break a leaf, pursue the dry stubble? Is it for thy honour to trample upon one that is down already, or to crush one that neither has nor pretends to any power to resist thee?" And Henry turns the plea into a ground of hope, for we ought to have such an apprehension of the goodness and compassion of God as to believe that he will not break the bruised reed (Matt. 12:20). The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's argument is drawn from his own weakness, that a leaf, a wisp of stubble, a bruised reed, is no fit adversary for the Almighty, and that the very smallness of the sufferer is a reason to look for pity rather than pursuit. It is the appeal of helplessness to a mercy that, the witnesses believe, does not delight to crush what is already broken.
26:
Job traces his present grief to an old reckoning reopened: "thou writest bitter things against me, and makest me to possess the iniquities of my youth." The reformed John Gill will not let the "bitter things" be sins recorded, since Job is at this very moment asking to be told his sins and denying any heinous ones; they must rather be afflictions, which are bitter and grievous and not joyous, and such especially as Job endured, these being what God is said to write against him. The wesleyan-arminian voices read the writing as a legal sentence. Adam Clarke: "The indictment is filled with bitter or grievous charges, which, if proved, would bring me to bitter punishment"; and of the second clause, "the levities and indiscretions of my youth I acknowledge, but is this a ground on which to form charges against a man the integrity of whose life is unimpeachable?" John Wesley glosses "writest" as "thou appointest or inflictest," a metaphor from princes or judges who anciently wrote down their sentences.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply marks the tone, calling the confession "exquisitely plaintive and affecting," for Job neither denies the sins of his youth nor thinks them cause enough for such a doom. Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the same strophe, feel the perplexity beneath it: Job can only take his affliction as the inheritance of youthful sins, since he has no sins of his mature years to reproach himself with, and cannot understand why God should again bring to account what he had long ago repented of.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the doctrine of it. God sometimes writes very bitter things against the best of his servants, in outward affliction and inward disquiet alike, that he may humble them and prove them and do them good in their latter end; and the sins of youth are often the smart of age, both in the sorrow within and the suffering without (Jer. 31:18-19), for time does not wear out the guilt of sin. When God writes such bitter things, Henry says, his design is to make us possess our iniquities, to bring forgotten sins to mind, and so to work in us such remorse as breaks us off from them; this is all the fruit, to take away sin. The witnesses do not divide over the pathos; they part only on the "bitter things" themselves, whether, with Gill, the grievous afflictions God inscribes against him, or, with Clarke and Wesley, the charges of an indictment, and all agree that Job feels the strange severity of a God who seems to have kept the record of a boy's faults to press upon a broken old man.
27:
"Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks" — Job pictures himself a prisoner watched at every step, and the witnesses work at both the image and a real difficulty in its grammar. The reformed John Gill takes the stocks as the punishment of offenders, a security against escape and a reservation for further punishment; so Job looked on his afflictions as a punishment for he knew not what, hemming him in so that he could no more get free than a man whose feet are fast in the stocks, and holding him for greater afflictions still, which he dreaded. Gill notes Aben Ezra's alternative, "thou puttest my feet in lime," so that Job's steps might be marked and easily traced as footprints in lime are; but he thinks this foreign to Job's mind, who would never concede that his steps, if taken amiss, were so visible.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the picture from life. The word means "in a clog," such as was tied to the feet of slaves to keep them from running away, still used, he says, among the slave-dealers of the West Indies, where it is called "the pudding," a great iron collar locked round the ankle; and he tells of a slave so long condemned to carry one that, when at last it was struck off, he could not walk without it until practice had taught him his balance again. "And lookest narrowly" means, thou hast seen all my goings out and comings in, so that no step of my life is unknown to thee; and "thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet" Clarke reads either of the mark the clog leaves, or of God pursuing him as a hound pursues its game by the scent.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses a genuine difficulty in the pronouns of these two verses, illustrated though the imprisonment be by the language of the Psalms (Ps. 88:8; Ps. 142:7). Some take the subject to be the fetter itself, "thou puttest my feet in the fetter that watcheth over all my paths, and imprinteth itself upon the roots of my feet, and it consumeth like a rotten thing"; others refer the "he" to Job himself, and others to man, the subject of the next chapter. In the Hebrew future the third person feminine and the second person masculine are alike, and the word for fetter, found only here and where Elihu quotes it in Job 33:11, may be feminine here; so that, Ellicott judges, the "he" introduced so abruptly is probably the object of all this watching and persecution. The witnesses do not finally divide; they agree that Job feels himself a marked and shackled man, his every path dogged, his very footprints noted, by a God whose scrutiny has become, to his darkened sense, a jailer's vigilance.
28:
The chapter ends on the frailty of the flesh, a body wasting like cloth in a chest: "he, as a rotten thing, consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten." The reformed John Gill notes that some Jewish writers tie the verse back to the driven leaf and dry stubble of v.25, and reads it of Job's own body: this frail and weakened frame, like any rotten thing, a rotten tree, as Ben Melech has it, is consuming and wasting away, clothed with worms and clods of dust. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the same sense. Adam Clarke: "I am like a vessel made of skin, rotten because of old age, or like a garment corroded by the moth," the reading the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic all followed, the "he" referring to Job himself. John Wesley marks the odd third person, noting that Job "speaks of himself in the third person, as is usual in this and other sacred books," so that "he, this poor frail creature, this body of mine," which perhaps Job pointed at with his finger, "consumeth or pineth away."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry allows the verse both ways, "he," that is man, consuming of himself like a moth-eaten garment whose principle of decay is in itself and which grows continually worse and worse, or else "He," that is God, consuming Job like rottenness and like a moth, and sets it beside the word of Hosea, "I will be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness" (Hos. 5:12). Man at the best, Henry says, wears fast, but under God's rebukes especially he is soon gone; and while there is so little soundness in the soul, it is no marvel there is so little soundness in the flesh (Ps. 38:3). The frame that seemed so strong is, in the end, but a garment the moth is quietly fretting away.

The witnesses do not divide; they close the chapter where Job's grief has been tending all along, on the moth-eaten garment of a life that seems to be rotting off him thread by thread, and on the strange spectacle of a man who, feeling himself thus consumed, has nevertheless just staked that consuming life on the God who both wounds and, he still believes, will save. The lament ends in decay, but not in despair, for the same speech that owns the moth has also owned the Redeemer.
